Soil sampling is shifting to data-driven models

See how you can fine-tune your soil sampling routine to someday align with high-tech models that yield more accurate results.

Allison Lynch,Staff Writer,Indiana Prairie FarmerAugust 26, 2026

schedule3 Min Read

A move to more data-driven soil sampling grids could transform the task. The biggest challenge will be overcoming bias to create accurate models.Tom J. Bechman 

Pulling soil samples by soil type alone may be a thing of the past as artificial intelligence continues trickling into agriculture. The move could make for more accurate soil test results and ultimately better-informed decisions, said Rodney Rulon.

“There’s a big push now, especially with AI and new technologies, to move that way,” said Rulon, a farmer from Arcadia, Ind. “So a lot of people, to keep the number of samples down but to increase accuracy, have been doing a lot of these ‘adjusted grid samples’ — a variation of the old soil type sampling — over the last few years.”

A new approach

These adjusted grid samples, still in their infancy, combine soil type and yield history to predict the most accurate spots to pull soil samples.

“You don’t necessarily just take them 330 feet apart — which is a 2.5 acre grid — or 500 feet apart,” Rulon added. “You adjust where you’ll take them in the field. And that makes a lot of sense to me if you have an unbiased basis to put those on.”

Related:Check off soil health to-do list during harvest downtime

Rulon has pulled samples on a 1-acre grid since returning to his family’s farm in the early 1990s, and he’s now working to incorporate AI in his soil sampling routine since he’s banked over 30 years’ worth of soil test data.

“We’re looking at, ‘Can we use that data and what’s been happening in the fields the last few years to create a modified sample that actually statistically represents what’s going on in the field?’” he explained. “And it’s not biased on what I think is going on in the field.”

That’s the challenge with this evolved approach to soil sampling; the data needs to guide the model, not your personal experiences and biases.

“That’s a big problem you can get into,” Rulon said. “Mentally, I think I know what’s going on in the field. So if I set up the sample points purely on what I think I’m going to represent, that may not be what the actual issue is.”

Collect accurate data

Before you can tap into those tools, Rulon explained that the foundation starts with collecting representative soil samples that will generate usable data. For him, the easiest place to start is by sampling on grids under 2.5 acres.

“In areas like ours, where there’s historic farm practice differences and different soil types in one field, a 2.5-acre grid would have 50% to 60% accuracy,” he said. “When you go down to a 1-acre grid, which is a 210-foot square, that gets you up to more like an 80% to 85% confidence and representation of that variability. It’s a big jump.”

There are two variables to factor into your sampling: special representation and temporal representation. Ensure you find a balance between how many samples you pull and how often you sample.

Related:Dive into the world of soil beneath your feet

“We went to the 1-acre grids, so we were getting what we felt was statistically superior data,” Rodney explained. “But we went to doing it less often. So instead of sampling every three years, we went to every four years.”

Fine-tuning your soil sampling routine now to collect valuable data could pay off as sampling models shift. Rulon urged folks to revisit their sampling routine as technology keeps evolving and don’t keep your agronomist out of the conversation.

“I think there’s a place for this technology if you have unbiased base map data — soil type maps and 1-acre grid maps and all these other sensors for organic matter and everything we have available now,” Rulon said. “I think there will be a place moving forward where we can create an unbiased, modified grid so you don’t have to take so many samples.”

About the Author

Allison Lynch

Staff Writer, Indiana Prairie Farmer

Allison Lynch, formerly Allison Lund, is a staff writer for Indiana Prairie Farmer. She graduated from Purdue University with a major in agricultural communications and a minor in crop science. She served as president of Purdue’s Agricultural Communicators of Tomorrow chapter. In 2022, she received the American FFA Degree.

Lynch grew up as the oldest of four children on a cash grain farm in south-central Wisconsin, where the primary crops were corn, soybeans, wheat and alfalfa. Her family also raised chewing tobacco and Hereford cattle. She spent most of her time helping with the tobacco crop in the summer and raising Boer goats for FFA projects. She now lives near Winamac, Ind, where her husband farms with his family.

translationZh:
仅按土壤类型采集土壤样本的做法可能成为过去，因为人工智能正不断渗透农业。印第安纳州阿卡迪亚的农民罗德尼·鲁隆表示，这一转变可能带来更准确的土壤测试结果，并最终促成更明智的决策。

“现在有一股强大的推动力，尤其是借助AI和新技术，正朝着那个方向发展，”鲁隆说。“所以很多人为了在减少样本数量的同时提高准确性，在过去几年里一直在做大量这种‘调整网格采样’——这是旧式土壤类型采样的一种变体。”

**一种新方法**

这些调整网格采样仍处于起步阶段，它结合了土壤类型和产量历史，来预测最准确的土壤采样点。

“你不一定非要每隔330英尺（即2.5英亩网格）或500英尺取一次样，”鲁隆补充道。“你可以调整田间采样点的位置。如果你有一个无偏见的依据来布置这些点，我觉得这很有意义。”

相关阅读：利用收获空闲期完成土壤健康待办清单

自上世纪90年代初回到家族农场以来，鲁隆一直在1英亩的网格上采样，由于他已经积累了超过30年的土壤测试数据，他现在正致力于将AI融入他的土壤采样程序中。

“我们在研究，‘我们能否利用这些数据以及过去几年田间发生的情况，来创建一个经过修正的、能在统计上真正代表田间状况的样本？’”他解释道。“而且它不受我个人对田间状况判断的影响。”

这就是这种进化后的土壤采样方法所面临的挑战；需要由数据来引导模型，而不是你的个人经验和偏见。

“这可能会成为一个大问题，”鲁隆说。“在思想上，我觉得自己了解田间的情况。所以，如果我纯粹根据自认为能代表的情况来设置采样点，那可能并非实际存在的问题所在。”

**收集准确数据**

鲁隆解释说，在你能利用这些工具之前，基础始于采集能生成可用数据的代表性土壤样本。对他来说，最简单的起点是在小于2.5英亩的网格上采样。

“在我们这样的地区，由于历史耕作方式的差异以及同一块田地里存在不同的土壤类型，2.5英亩网格的准确率大约只有50%到60%，”他说。“当你缩小到1英亩网格，即210英尺见方，置信度和对变异性的代表性就能提升到大约80%到85%。这是一个巨大的飞跃。”

采样时需要考虑两个变量：空间代表性和时间代表性。确保在采样数量和采样频率之间找到平衡。

相关阅读：探索脚下的土壤世界

“我们采用了1英亩网格，因此我们获得了自认为在统计上更优越的数据，”罗德尼解释说。“但我们降低了采样频率。因此，我们不是每三年采样一次，而是改为每四年一次。”

现在微调你的土壤采样程序以收集有价值的数据，随着采样模型的转变，未来可能会得到回报。鲁隆敦促人们在技术不断发展的过程中重新审视他们的采样程序，并且不要让农艺师缺席讨论。

“我认为这项技术有它的用武之地，前提是你有无偏见的底图数据——土壤类型图、1英亩网格图，以及我们现在可用的所有其他用于检测有机质等的传感器，”鲁隆说。“我认为未来会有那么一个位置，让我们能够创建一个无偏见的、经过修正的网格，这样你就不必采集那么多样本了。”
contentHtml: See how you can fine-tune your soil sampling routine to someday align with high-tech models that yield more accurate results.
